items.question: What do you see as the limitations of grounding AI alignment in preferences and expected utility maximization?
items.object: The preference-based view of AI alignment
items.answer: What we argue in a paper, Beyond Preferences in AI Alignment, is that we are really trying to critique this preferences view. We go through all the limitations of taking this expected utility maximization view of both human rationality and AI alignment too seriously. People know that this learned utility function you try and learn from preference data doesn't perfectly capture what people really want, and that leads to issues of overoptimization because it is a bad proxy for what humans might supposedly really want in that context. Overoptimizing it is not going to get you there.

items.question: What drew you to AI alignment given your reservations about effective altruism's moral argument for working on it?
items.object: Effective altruism and the intellectual appeal of AI value learning
items.answer: I encountered an effective altruist club as part of my undergraduate degree in the U.S. I actually ran it for a bit, despite always having been slightly too leftist to really buy in fully to effective altruism. That's when I encountered a lot of ideas around AI safety and alignment. Basically, the way I describe it is, I wasn't necessarily convinced of the moral argument for working on this as the most important thing from an effective altruist's point of view, or utilitarian point of view, but it just seemed like a really interesting question because I was already a big fan of moral philosophy. This project of, “How could you begin to computationally model value learning? What does it mean to specify a computational process for learning human values? items.question: How has your postcolonial perspective shaped your view of which philosophical traditions matter for AI alignment?
items.object: Postcolonial thinking and philosophical pluralism in AI alignment
items.answer: I do think, in fact, all thinkers are regional thinkers, whether they know it or not. But I think the way I've approached that question has been influenced, I don't know, by perhaps my cultural, political, national background in various ways. I do think of myself as a postcolonial thinker, I suppose, and part of that manifests in a general distrust towards Western philosophy and Western-centered philosophy as the sole source of philosophical knowledge about what could possibly be relevant to thinking about how to AI-align AI. A nice representation of that view is a talk I gave maybe almost five years ago on the relevance of philosophical pluralism for alignment: how ideas from, say, Buddhist philosophy or Confucian philosophy could be relevant to thinking and talking about what it means to align our systems of human values. items.question: How do you prefer to frame forecasts of AI progress given your reservations about the concept of AGI?
items.object: AGI as a concept and a basis for forecasting AI progress
items.answer:
First of all, I don't even really like the concept of AGI. I think it's too amorphous to really pinpoint what we're talking about. I kind of prefer thinking about things in terms of, like, really impactful: what would it take to automate the industrial economy, or automate even 50 to 80% of the existing industrial economy? Because I think more industries will come to exist in the future. In principle—not even actually, because I think there are a lot of regulatory or societal reasons why a lot of technology we develop won't actually be deployed—and if that's the way of thinking about AI, then I think we are not going to get there for a decade or two, is my guess, or more.

I do in principle believe it's possible to automate a lot of the existing industrial economy and a lot of the cognitive work that goes into running it within the century. But it does seem to me that a lot of the particular predictions or beliefs of large AI companies like OpenAI are, firstly, predicated on the particular vision of what AGI means, and also, even within that, too optimistic.

items.question: Why do you think motor intelligence deserves more weight in discussions of AGI?
items.object: Motor intelligence and robotics in definitions of AGI
items.answer: One way I think about that is thinking about particular sectors of the global economy, and that way I have better intuitions about how long it would take. So much of the global economy is still manual labor, physical labor, but that is a hard intelligence problem to solve. I think people really underrate how much of human and animal intelligence was dedicated to solving hard motor tasks. We need a lot of motor intelligence to solve that. I think what has happened by people defining AGI to talk about cognitive labor, whatever that means, is that they've gerrymandered out most of robotics, when that's such an important part of what you might think of as human intelligence and a really important part of the global economy. items.question: How do you assess the prospect of AI systems automating science and remote office work anytime soon?
items.object: AI automation of science and remote office work
items.answer:
I think the part of the economy that a lot of AI companies seem to be focused on when trying to achieve something like AGI is much more like what people use metaphors like “drop-in remote workers” for. I didn't know it was a metaphor, but that's a rough sense of what will be achieved. They also talk about—I can't remember what Dario Amodei's metaphor was recently—like a country of geniuses in a data center or something like that. That's pointing to a particular set of cognitive capacities. I do think we're seeing a lot more progress on those things, but to me there's a big open question whether either of them is going to happen anytime soon.

One is science: a country of geniuses in a data center is automating science of a certain kind, or the idea-generation parts of science and experimental planning. Of course, you still have to do all the stuff with the actual machines and run the experiments, and that's going to be slow. The remote worker stuff is all the general cognitive tasks a remote office worker has to do on a computer to achieve a certain job. Even on that simpler task, I think this really depends on how much we believe a lot of office work needs very high reliability. The current paradigm of scaling AI systems based on large language models is not on track to achieve the 95 to 99% reliability levels you might want from doing that kind of job. If the standards of reliability happen to be looser, it might be the case—some kinds of roles are like that. If you're talking about copywriting, I think that kind of work can be automated. But if it's much more precise or requires certain kinds of standards of precision, I don't really think pure language models with a bit of stuff added on are the right tool.

items.question: How do you understand the gap between preference-based theories of AI alignment and the way developers actually train language models?
items.object: Preference-based theories of AI alignment and the practice of training language models
items.answer:
The theory, the dominant theory we have for thinking and talking about that if you read these papers on AI alignment, is essentially a preferences one, where the idea is that there's some utility function or reward function in people's heads that captures those preferences, captures a linear ordering over how good outputs are. People are expressing that linear ordering over how good outputs are by making these judgments, and they're expressing it noisily sometimes. There is room for noise when they make these kinds of judgments; there are Boltzmann-rational assumptions about how people may or may not always pick the best option because we're not perfectly rational. But the basic assumption is that we have a linear ordering in our head and express it, and we're going to align the AI system ideally to optimize that underlying linear order or utility function. There is some sequence of outputs; we want the AI system to try and output the best one in general.

Even though that's the theory, I think the practice is better understood as not actually doing that. We talk about it that way, but that's not what AI developers actually want for AI systems, and it's not what they're implicitly doing. First of all, people quite explicitly don't actually try and maximize this learned utility function or reward function to the extreme. People know that this learned utility function that you try and learn from preference data doesn't perfectly capture what people really want, and it leads to issues of overoptimization because it is a bad proxy for what humans might supposedly really want. Overoptimizing it is not going to get you there. The AI systems trained to maximize the reward function are only partly trained, constrained to be close to the original base policy of the original non-finetuned language model to some degree. This process is iterative, so you keep trying to make your language model a little better in terms of better complying with human preferences, but you're always constraining it to be somewhat closer to the original distribution.

That already is a departure from the traditional theory, which is maximize expected utility.

items.question: How do you think preference data should relate to normative standards in aligning AI assistants?
items.object: Normative standards and the role of preference data in aligning AI assistants
items.answer:
I don't think the right way to understand what assistants are doing is maximizing utility at all. The developers had in mind a set of system requirements or normative standards for how they want their conversational AI system to behave. They want it to be helpful and harmless. Those are two very broad, vague normative standards, but if you look at something like constitutional AI, they're much more specific ones, like don't be toxic, try to respond in a way that encourages reflection, things like that. They have this whole list of standards, and they're either getting people or AI systems to make judgments that comply with those standards. They're trying to aggregate those judgments somehow and align the AI system to that.

There's a difference between using preference data and measuring it as a way to learn information about how to follow these normative standards, and treating preferences as an alignment target. What our paper is trying to do is critique the idea that preferences should be the alignment target, as opposed to merely data we can use to learn about the things that humans really care about. That's my broad response to how I think about what people are actually doing nowadays. There's a sense in which the way we're thinking and talking about the actual practice is a bad one, and we're doing something else that's richer.

items.question: How do you understand the conceptual paradigm behind reinforcement learning from human feedback and inverse reinforcement learning?
items.object: The utility-maximization paradigm of AI alignment
items.answer:
I think they're a particular technical and conceptual paradigm for thinking about aligning systems. It starts from this picture of AI systems not as any kind of program but as expected utility maximizers, an idea that goes back to Yudkowsky: the right way to think of intelligence is to think of it as maximizing some utility function in expectation. If you think of AI systems in that way, then aligning AI must be about getting the right utility function. How do we learn that utility function? Clearly we should want it to be something like the human utility function, so let's assume human utility functions exist. How have economists and decision theorists traditionally thought of these utility functions? As certain kinds of preference orderings which comply with certain kinds of axioms of rationality. So we're going to try and learn from actually expressed preferences to recover the utility function and get the system to optimize for that.

If you take AI alignment to be that, there are a whole ton of philosophical and practical problems to solve. Our paper goes through them in detail, and I do think the ones you brought up are serious ones for that view of AI alignment.

items.question: Why do you think aligning large language models is better understood as aligning them to normative standards?
items.object: Large language model alignment as alignment to normative standards
items.answer:
What I was trying to say earlier is that we are not really training AI systems—well, some AI systems we are training in that way—but large language models don't really have that flavor. Firstly, I don't think it's right to think of them as expected utility maximizers. They're particular programs or neural networks that can be thought of as policies; they sample tokens as they go. The way you describe the policy, it's quite hard to describe it as maximizing some expected utility. It's not actually doing that in general. So that's already an issue. When you train them, you don't actually train them to maximize a specific utility function; you push them in that direction, but you're not pushing them all the way.

There's a sense in which theory and practice come apart. In some ways what we're trying to do with the paper is point out that the practice is better understood by this other kind of thing we described, which is aligning AI systems to normative standards. That's what we're already doing without realizing it, and that's what we should do, is also something we argue.

items.question: How do you understand the significance of using KL regularization to keep a reinforcement-trained language model close to its original policy?
items.object: KL regularization in language model reinforcement learning
items.answer:
I do think it's a meaningful difference because it really does affect the theory of how these systems work. It is the case, quite explicitly from the way people are training it, that they're not actually at training time maximizing a particular scalar. They are maximizing this different scalar objective, but it's not the one that characterizes human preferences. They're doing some mix of imitation learning and using reward maximization.

People have written papers about how there's a sense in which imitation learning from humans, which is how pretrained language models are trained—they do imitation learning from the web, essentially—is much safer because presumably humans don't do, at least, extinction-risk-level unsafe things on the internet. If you just imitate that, you're going to pick up everything, and tons of other gross, nasty stuff, but you're not going to pick up the pathological behaviors that can come from optimizing a thing that doesn't capture human values very well with a lot of power.

I think the KL objective, the KL-regularized objective where you constrain the policy to be close to the original policy, is a way of doing that. It says we don't fully trust this proxy of what humans care about, and so we're going to interpolate between the original thing, which is imitate what humans do, and do what humans say is better. I think that makes language models less subject to classical risks that people have theorized apply to expected utility maximizers.

items.question: Why do you see social roles as a useful way to define what AI alignment should aim for?
items.object: Social roles as a target for AI alignment
items.answer:
We go through all the limitations of really taking this expected utility maximization view of both human rationality and AI alignment too seriously. I think there are a lot of issues with that. A lot of it comes from thinking about what we want AI systems to do for us in the first place. We often do want them to play particular social functions and social roles for us. This has traditionally been the case of systems we think of as tools. Most technology we build serves as tools or services for us, and when they're tools or services, they have a clearly defined social functional role that they ought to play well, ideally.

Even as they become more agentic, and more like personal assistants that talk to us over long periods of time or execute tasks over long-range horizons for us, I think we still think and talk about what social functional role we want them to play. From that perspective, it becomes much more clear what alignment should be. If you think of them as playing certain social functions and roles, then the normative target is: what does it mean to play that social functional role well? What are the standards, constraints, and system requirements for a system that's supposed to play this role?

items.question: How do you think about the social role of general-purpose AI assistants?
items.object: General-purpose AI assistants as a new social role
items.answer:
In the paper we go into more detail about a specific case a lot of people working on AGI or large language models are excited about: general-purpose AI assistants. I think that's just one kind of thing an AI system could do. It's strange to think of that as the only thing an AI system could do, whereas a lot of AGI talk seems to fall into this pattern of building the one system that's going to do everything for everyone. I don't think that's going to be the case. A personal assistant is one kind of thing you can do, and that's going to have certain kinds of normative standards we want to figure out that it should comply with.

Part of that work is something we have to do as a society. We kind of know what human personal assistants should do, and we can apply some of those normative standards to a personal assistant. But we're creating a fundamentally new kind of social role or function with these systems, and we have to collectively figure out politically what these systems ought to do. There's also the technical problem: once we've figured out those standards, how do we get systems to reliably comply with them?

items.question: How do you approach choosing methods to make AI systems comply with normative standards?
items.object: Methods for getting AI systems to comply with normative standards
items.answer:
There are a bunch of ways to do that. You can use traditional machine learning techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback, constitutional AI, where you get people to demonstrate what it means to comply with certain kinds of normative standards. There are cases where you can formalize those standards. For example, if you're building a very different kind of system, a household robot, there are basic standards we want to apply: don't collide with people; don't break my fragile objects in my house. Those things are much more amenable to formalization in a formal world model of how houses work, with 3D objects in a room: this is what it means for a mug to be broken, this is what it means to be too close to a human. We can write down those specifications or partly learn them, and then use planning algorithms to guarantee safety with respect to those constraints.

It's worth separating the normative target, how we specify it formally or informally, and how we actually get an AI system to comply with that. I think it's going to be really different depending on what kind of AI system we're building and what we want it to do.

items.question: How do you think about the different products and roles that make up the AI economy?
items.object: The AI economy's distinct products and roles
items.answer:
A general-purpose, instructable robot in your household is one system you might want to build, quite different from a general-purpose conversational assistant. I think it's going to be different from a general-purpose automated researcher, and different from many other things people are already building: automated traders, flight-booking assistants, customer-service agents. Governments might want to deploy agents that talk to users about how to access a government service. Those are all pretty different kinds of things. Many are built nowadays by taking a single underlying model and customizing it. That's one way; you can also do more traditional natural-language programming techniques.

There's the product, the end-user product, and then there's the business-to-business product, which is the model. That itself is a different product you can put a box around. If I'm a developer trying to build models I can sell to other businesses, what are the normative requirements for that? That's how I think about the space of the AI economy. I could list even more things: AI for energy redistribution, controlling drones, data analysis, scientific simulation and inference. I work a bit more in this space because I work in probabilistic programming, which is about scaling up various forms of Bayesian data analysis, but also applications like AI-based 3D perception.

items.question: How do you think negative externalities change what AI systems should owe to people beyond their users?
items.object: Political disagreement over AI alignment standards and negative externalities
items.answer:
I think a lot of the problems we have from political conflict largely don't arise when you have decentralization. Insofar as AI systems serve particular users—individuals or companies or organizations—the primary alignment target is what the user or organization wants out of it.

The problem is that these systems aren't just going to benefit or provide value for individual users or organizations; they're also going to have negative externalities on the rest of the world, depending on what we allow people to use systems for. For example, we presumably don't want individual users to learn how to make a pipe bomb from Claude very easily, because that would make terrorist attacks happen more frequently, perhaps. That's where we need to start thinking about these questions, which really become politically contested because they're about restricting individuals' ability to perform certain tasks so that we don't harm other people. Of course people have very different opinions on where to draw the line. Given that people disagree, we need fair and impartial ways of deciding what these standards are going to be.

Practically, what we need is first to figure out political and social institutions for getting what people want—what standards or principles people really want to govern systems which have negative externalities—into the hands of developers, and perhaps create incentives for developers to implement systems that comply with those standards. That's a big part of what governance is supposed to solve.

items.question: Why do you prefer Scanlon's contractualism to Rawls's veil of ignorance when thinking about what AI should owe to us?
items.object: Scanlon's contractualism and Rawls's veil of ignorance
items.answer:
I think this question, “What should AI owe to us?” really borrows from the contractualist tradition in Western political philosophy. Rawls is a major thinker in this, but the phrase is more associated with other philosophers, Tim Scanlon. He puts forward the idea of the basic way to figure out what we owe to each other—he's talking about what humans or people owe to each other—is to think about general principles, which you can extend to acts: what kinds of actions or principles could we live by that no one could reasonably reject? “Reasonably reject” is doing a lot of work here; it can mean so many things.

That general picture is a bit in contrast to this Rawlsian veil-of-ignorance view. One way you could do that, which we allude to in the paper, is using a Rawlsian approach. There are many others. Philosophers have spent so much time trying to figure out how you should do political philosophy. Practically speaking, I don't really like this veil-of-ignorance thing, because I think it presumes there is this disembodied person you could be before entering the world. That seems weird, not actually practical, and not coherent. I think the kinds of things we care about are always deeply socially embedded. I'm more of a fan of Scanlon's view.

items.question: What do you find compelling about Jillian Hadfield and Dylan Hadfield-Menell's paper “AI Alignment and the Incomplete Contracting Problem”?
items.object: AI Alignment and the Incomplete Contracting Problem
items.answer:
The more interesting technical question is: if you take these politically negotiated normative standards as the alignment target, some of that we'll be able to do offline in advance through a political process. But as systems become more complex or autonomous, sometimes you're going to have to build systems that figure out what society would agree to on their own to some degree. Jillian Hadfield, in a paper with Dylan Hadfield-Menell called “AI Alignment and the Incomplete Contracting Problem,” puts this really well.

We don't just want AI systems to learn and predict user preferences; what they need to do is learn, predict, and respond to society's normative infrastructure. A lot of the contracts we implicitly have with AI systems, whether individual contracts between two parties or contracts with society as a whole, have missing clauses. They're never going to be complete. We often have to figure out how we should fill in the contract when we enter those situations. Part of how we do this is through law and the courts, but before going to court, we often hire lawyers to figure out what we should do so we can avoid going to court. I think that kind of capability is going to be important if we're going to build systems with really autonomous, wide scope.

items.question: Why do you still find Eric Drexler's Comprehensive AI Services report relevant to the future of AI?
items.object: Eric Drexler's Comprehensive AI Services report
items.answer:
I think Drexler's Comprehensive AI Services report has been really influential for my thinking ever since I read it, and I still think it's relevant for a bunch of reasons. Firstly, we already have a whole bunch of narrow superhuman systems, and none of them even look like things like AlphaZero. They look like your Google Maps routing algorithm. That's one of the most classic AI algorithms we have: search for spatial navigation. Those basic algorithms are used every day when you run a search on Google Maps or Apple Maps to get from point A to point B, and they're way better than human navigators could be. They can do it at far greater scale.

A lot of the economy we've automated, as things become solved, we stop calling AI and start calling it computer science or software engineering. There's a lot of stuff we've already automated in ways we've made superhuman, and I think there's reason to think that trend will continue in many domains.

There's a question whether, concurrent with that continuing, something like Dario's picture of automated AI scientists or drop-in remote workers will happen from really large, monolithic, general-purpose AI systems. The trajectory of general-purpose systems is still somewhat open to me, but I tend to be on the side that we can probably still afford to do better by specialization.

items.question: Why do you think specialized AI systems could outperform monolithic models even if those models first succeed at automating science?
items.object: Specializing central cognition into modular AI services
items.answer:
I think the basic picture of what AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI think they're doing is automating what some cognitive scientists might call central cognition, as opposed to more specialized mental modules for a particular task. Specialized mental modules might be for perception, spatial planning or navigation, theory of mind, or intuitive physics prediction. These are things human babies have from a very young age; animals have them too. Core knowledge is what Elizabeth Spelke calls this. Then there are other kinds of specialized expertise we learn as we get older.

It doesn't seem like the large AI companies are thinking they're going to get all those things. The primary delta or comparative advantage of the systems they're trying to build seems to be central cognition: general reasoning and planning or problem-solving abilities at a high, abstract level, not mechanistic reasoning where you know all the rules—in that case Python interpreters or proof-search engines will be a lot better—or general knowledge retrieval at a relevant point, and a huge amount of working memory to bring together all the relevant information and disparate considerations into solving a new problem, the kind of thing you presumably need to do science well.

To me, it's an open scientific and engineering question: maybe even if large-language-model-plus systems like o1 get to be the first systems that replicate many aspects of human central cognition well enough to serve as drop-in remote workers or automate science, how sure are we that we can't do better by specializing? If cognitive scientists who are proponents of the modularity thesis or massive modularity are right that there is no single thing as central cognition, that all specialized modules interact in particular ways, and if we can eventually reverse-engineer those modules, or AI systems can help us do that, then the specialized modules are going to do a lot better. If you can get them to do better, they're going to be smaller, cheaper, more efficient, perhaps more reliable if you work out the underlying logic. They'll get the benefits of economic and computational specialization we already see with today's systems.

If we figure out how to specialize those aspects of what we currently call central cognition, then perhaps even if o1-plus ends up being the first kind of system to achieve those tasks, we'll rapidly figure out cheaper, better, more specialized ways of doing it by reverse-engineering the specific mental capacities required, recomposing systems out of them, and serving and deploying those systems instead. That's my picture of how things will play out even if these large monolithic systems win out. It feels more realistic when you think that humans like cognitive scientists and AI researchers could do that work. You might be skeptical of how quickly we can do that, but if we're going to get AI systems that can automate science eventually, specializing code or figuring out cognitive science is one of the things humans do well. Why would a monolithic system do better than systems that specialize to do specialization, modular system building, and other specialized tasks?

That's my pitch for the more services-cell view of how AI will go in the future. items.question: How do you understand constitutional AI's relationship to contractualist approaches to AI alignment?
items.object: Constitutional AI as an implementation of contractualist AI alignment
items.answer: I think of constitutional AI—one way to think of the character design is that's virtue ethics, but I don't think it's just that. When you think about building moral systems, I think there's a certain kind of thing you want to comply with: a basic kind of minimal morality that the system should comply to, which is meet the minimum moral standards that society would agree to allow you to operate. That's going to be filled in by the contractualist picture. I think constitutional AI is a bit closer to that, because if you look at the kinds of principles they're framing, they're things that approximately liberal people would agree should govern a conversational AI assistant. This collective constitutional AI paper that followed up explicitly did that: they surveyed Americans on principles and what the AI should do, took the views that were agreed upon most, and found a set of principles that disagreeing groups agreed upon most to build a publicly sourced constitution. I think that's close to one way of instantiating the contractualist AI alignment idea we advance in the paper.

items.question: How do you think AI systems should work out what principles govern their behavior in novel situations that a fixed constitution does not cover?
items.object: Online normative reflection for AI systems encountering novel situations
items.answer:
I think constitutional AI has limits. One is that this is a one-off process, and you might worry that's not enough if these systems enter novel situations where people didn't specify principles covering that case. That's modulo making sure we even understand the meanings of these principles well enough to get the AI system to comply. The surprising part of constitutional AI is that you can use the AI system itself to produce preference judgments according to those principles, align to that, and turn it into a scalar objective to maximize. But even modulo that, there are questions of what you do out of distribution. In those cases, automated reflection upon what kinds of principles should govern your behavior in this new situation comes into play. It's no longer this offline process that constitutional AI delivers; it's a more online process. The AI has to say, “I don't have data from humans right now, but I have my own capacity to think about what other people would agree to, about how I should act.” That's an open area for research. Game theory, moral philosophy, and studies of human moral cognition have a lot to offer, and political philosophy certainly does. That's part of what we advocate for in the paper.

There's a lot of room to get more precise. Part of why we didn't get even more precise is that once you make things precise, you make certain implicit ethical or representational commitments which might be the wrong ones, and we want to encourage people to explore more broadly. One way to do it is the traditional game-theoretic view: if you have a sense of what people tend to favor or disfavor, you can simulate how they would bargain. This technique is known as virtual bargaining, using a Nash bargaining solution to agree upon a standard. Or you could use something more Rawlsian. There's a recent paper by DeepMind called the H-MAS machine, where you get people to express their opinions and then get the AI system to come to a consensus statement. You can imagine a way to simulate people's opinions on how to act in a situation and synthesize a consensus policy from each individual's positions on what you should do on the fly. Both seem like reasonable ways to go, and you have to test them and figure out whether they'll work. The resulting consensus from virtual bargaining or Rawlsian deliberation can be what you actually align the AI system to.

items.question: How much of a departure from traditional AI alignment do you consider vector reward approaches to be?
items.object: Vector rewards and their relationship to traditional AI alignment
items.answer:
As for vector rewards, it feels a bit like not actually moving that far away from the traditional approach. The nice thing about vector rewards is that you're more explicit that different values trade off differently in different contexts. There's work on contextual preference modeling that tries to better model that: if you're an AI teacher, you're going to prioritize certain values more than others. Helpfulness as an AI teacher means something slightly different; you probably don't want to feed students the answer the way you would as a general-purpose encyclopedia assistant. Vector rewards are good for that, but I don't think they're a fundamental difference from the traditional framework because at the end of the day you're aggregating them into a single utility function, just with more representational clarity, interpretability, auditability, and governability. Those are good things, but it's not a fundamental difference.

What would be a fundamental difference is actually figuring out a theory of helpfulness, a theory of harmfulness, a theory of what it means to be a good teacher, a good robot of any kind, and building systems that can do that normative reasoning—whether that's formal or more like imitating humans. We talk a bit about that in the paper, but both seem really unexplored directions to me.

items.question: How did constitutional AI change your assessment of language models' ability to reason about normative principles?

items.answer: I'm going to admit straight out: I think they're surprisingly good. items.question: Where do you see the limits of large language models as advisers on ethical dilemmas and public policy?
items.object: Large language models as ethical advisers and policy evaluators
items.answer:
When it comes to conversationally helping people with resolving various kinds of moral and ethical dilemmas, I wouldn't be surprised if they actually do pretty well, as good as or better than a good friend. I think there are a host of other kinds of questions they're probably not going to do well at, which is not to say that any single human does well at them either. This is why we need other kinds of technologies to help us. Can Claude adequately assess the best kind of climate policy or immigration policy? I don't think it's going to be very good at giving the right answer, whatever that means, according to some standard of rightness. I do think it's going to be good at providing a whole list of considerations that any reasonable person should consider as they think about this for themselves.

In actually evaluating the effects of the policy, we need very different kinds of AI systems than what large language models are designed to do. We need pretty good scientific models of how the world works, and we're so far away from that for things as complex as climate policy. You have to build good enough climate models; you need to build good enough models of how society works. There are some kinds of things where we can make headway, and a lot of traditional social choice has been in this regime where you can define the payoff and cost well enough.

items.question: Why do you see learning shared normative constraints as a useful approach to aligning AI systems that act on behalf of different individuals and organizations?
items.object: Learning shared normative constraints as an approach to AI alignment
items.answer:
The basic picture is, if we take seriously this view that we're going to have tons of different AI systems out there, then we want them to largely pursue objectives on behalf of particular individuals and organizations. But of course if you do that too much, then there may be costs imposed on the rest of society. We can attempt to prespecify all the kinds of constraints an AI system should comply with in advance, by following existing law or something like that, but I think there's good reason to think that for some kinds of AI systems we won't be able to prespecify everything in advance. For things that are not formally specified, that are really local and contingent, or where there are ambiguous gaps in the law, the AI assistants will have to figure it out for themselves.

One way to figure out what shared normative constraints society shares is by learning from other people or other agents in the environment. This is a way to perform a kind of alignment that doesn't have the hard problem of figuring out every single agent's preferences and perfectly choosing the optimal plan that satisfies all of them. Instead, it's: I'm going to do my thing, constrained not to harm other people or society too much, and I'm going to figure out what the constraints are. That's one way of attempting to formalize some aspects of this more contractualist picture of AI alignment.

items.question: How do you understand the role of beliefs about other agents' behavior in helping AI agents learn and coordinate around social norms in your Markov-game framework?
items.object: Inferring social norms from other agents' behavior in a Markov game
items.answer:
To figure out what the constraints should be, we set it up using the formalism called the Markov game. This is a standard formalism used to describe multi-agent reinforcement-learning tasks. Essentially, you have a bunch of agents that each have their individual objectives. We're going to assume that's describable by a reward function. Traditional solution concepts in game theory are that the agents should converge to either a Nash equilibrium or correlated equilibrium, stable patterns of behavior such that no one would prefer to deviate from that joint pattern of behavior.

An interesting philosophical question is how that connects to what humans actually do: we seem to follow and obey social norms, and we seem to learn social norms from society. We made this extension to the Markov game that helps people coordinate upon better sets of norms, which you can think of as better equilibria, by giving them some initial beliefs about how the rest of society operates. These beliefs are: do I believe the rest of society is complying with a certain rule most of the time? We'll call that rule a norm. We'll have a set of possible rules, a whole space of possible rules. You can imagine a compositional language, a formal language, a programming language or natural language, for describing all those rules. I'm going to try to infer from people's behavior what rules they're following, and if I infer what rules they're following, hopefully I can comply with those rules as well.

If we build agents that have an intrinsic desire to comply with the rules they believe to be true—in the sense that the rest of society is complying with them—then we get this automatic behavior: I'm going to pursue my individual objective subject to the constraint of complying with rules it seems most of society is complying with right now. That's the basic picture we offer in that paper.

The agents model the other agents in the environment. They assume that most of the time they're trying to pursue their self-interest, like picking up apples, but sometimes other agents do weird things: “I guess they're not eating this apple, even though it seems like it'll be good for them to do so,” and they're also going to the river to clean it every once in a while. If you're Bayesian enough about this, you should infer that there are probably some rules out there they're following that explain this behavior, and update your beliefs about what those rules are based on the fact that they better explain other people's behavior than the hypothesis that they're maximizing only immediate self-interest.

items.question: How do you think anticipated sanctions could extend your norm-learning framework to agents that want to free-ride?

We don't explore this in the paper, but if I believe other people are going to comply with the norm and sanction me for not complying, then once I form a belief that this norm is practiced by the rest of society, I better comply with it for my own sake, at least insofar as I can't get away with breaking it. That extended version handles the fact that some agents want to free-ride and break the law.

items.question: What do you see as the main obstacle to generalizing your norm-learning framework from discrete simulations to richer real-world settings?
items.object: Generalizing the symbolic norm-learning framework beyond discrete simulated environments
items.answer:
I do think it can generalize. Discreteness for me is not the main issue. You can imagine the dirtiness of the river as a continuous variable. I also think when humans model the world, we often effectively discretize it in various ways to make our planning easier. We just don't think at the level of resolution of individual continuous variables. We often abstract the world into simpler high-level abstractions in order to do efficient planning, so that part is not an issue for me.

The bigger scalability bottleneck of that particular framework implementation is that it required an explicit formal model of the world in order to specify these symbolic rules to do learning over. There are a whole bunch of questions about expanding beyond that. A narrower regime would be a self-driving car that can learn driving conventions not only in San Francisco but also in Vietnam and India, where people drive really differently. It still seems possible you could have a good enough implicit world model of what it means to drive cars into situations, and a good enough model of how other agents would drive in your driving setting, so that you can infer local driving conventions in that richer space. That's an intermediate step: you need to write much richer world models, but it's still not as open-ended as what people want large language models to do.

items.question: How would you extend your norm-learning approach to language-model agents operating with rules expressed in natural language?
items.object: Using language models to infer and interpret natural-language norms
items.answer:

A big question then is the semantics of those natural-language rules. In the simulator we had a well-defined interpreter for what the rules mean; you can formally check what it means to break or not break the rule. With a large language model you don't have that, because you don't have a formal world model. One thing you could try—and there's a sense in which constitutional AI is doing this—is use the language model as a classifier for whether the rule is broken. You can take the log probability of the token “yes” or “no” to get a probabilistic estimate of whether the rule is broken, and maybe do the Bayesian thing we're doing.

One strategy would be to build an LM agent that looks at other agents and people in society and what they do, and prompt it to hypothesize a bunch of rules that might explain people's behavior in a setting. They might differ from its initial expectations or whatever; some prompt will probably come up with not entirely unreasonable hypotheses. Then you can rate them according to how well they explain the data. You can formalize this as an importance-sampling technique, a way to approximate Bayesian inference in this much richer space. You can do that process iteratively, perhaps. That's one thought about how to generalize in a couple directions.

items.question: How do you understand the role of thresholding in your formalism for agents deciding whether to follow norms?
items.object: Thresholding and sampling as approximations to norm-sensitive decision-making
items.answer:
We didn't just do thresholding; we also did sampling. There are a bunch of ways we set up the formalism. There's the ideal thing to do, and then there's the algorithm that practically tries to achieve the ideal but falls short in some degrees.

We set it up so that if you're an agent with infinite computation, you should be able to do Bayesian inference over the full space of possible norms. You should be able to assign a posterior probability to each rule or norm being true. Given that posterior probability, we have this belief-dependent reward function, which says: to the extent I believe a certain rule is true, I'm going to take myself to pay a cost. The norm-augmented reward function I'm trying to maximize is: I'm going to maximize my individual interest, subject to not suffering too much cost from violating the norm. If I only have 10% belief that this rule is active, practiced by society, I'm not going to care much about the cost. If I have 90% belief, I'm going to really care about the cost. That's the actual objective function the agents are supposed to aim for.

There are many ways to approximate maximization of that objective. One way is simple thresholding: if my belief in a certain rule is high enough, I follow it; if not, I don't. That's a simple heuristic that approximates the actual expected utility maximization in that context. Another thing you could do is sample and say, when you're really uncertain about the norms, maybe it's worth doing some exploration. You try breaking it, try not breaking it, and see how people respond. The agents don't really learn in that case, because we don't really have punishment in the simulation, but in principle exploration can help.

items.question: How do you think experimenting with possible norms can produce shared conventions when none initially exist?

items.answer: One thing I think experimentation can help with is if you're in a situation where you're not sure if any norms exist at all. Even though initially there wasn't a convention being followed, because people experimentally comply with certain rules, other people start seeing that and follow them, and they bootstrap off each other and converge on a shared set of norms. items.question: How would you model agents learning to stop following a social norm as it falls out of practice?
items.object: Norm decay through Bayesian inference about current social behavior
items.answer:
I would have agents, instead of trying to comply with something they think society's practicing over all time, try to comply with what society has been practicing for the last K time steps or something like that.

If you're going to update your beliefs as a Bayesian agent, you would gradually update: society's following these norms, society's following these norms; oh, it seems like other people stopped following these norms, maybe because it became too costly for them to comply, and then I would learn that society no longer complies with it and update my belief and start complying with that norm less. That's one way of capturing decay that falls out of doing inference over what society is currently complying with.

I do think people do this. Another example is people rapidly adapt to littering norms. If you see tons of litter on the ground, say right after a football match, you're like, “Okay, I guess I'm not expected to care about litter in this context; it's fine,” and you probably infer it's not a big deal if I also litter. Whereas you walk somewhere else and there are completely clean streets, and you're like, “Okay, I'm going to quickly adapt: in this part of town it's not okay to litter.”

items.question: How do you assess the social benefits and risks of people's intrinsic desire to comply with what others are doing?
items.object: Norm conformity and the persistence of oppressive norms
items.answer:
Oh, definitely no guarantee it converges to something good. There are plenty of bad equilibria and plenty of good equilibria. The mere fact that we have an intrinsic desire to comply with what other people are doing tends to be good because it allows us to converge to good equilibria that we wouldn't have been able to if we were always never doing that. But it also allows us to converge to much worse systems, or to stabilize systems that were initially good but turn out to be bad as environments change.

I think this is a big problem society struggles with, and there are many oppressive norms. One of the people we cite a lot is Christina Bicchieri; she's written a really nice book called The Grammar of Society. She writes about pluralistic ignorance: people still believe everyone else thinks they should follow the norm, but in fact they personally don't want to comply with it anymore. This happens in societies with oppressive norms that most people don't want, but they believe everyone else thinks they should follow and follow that norm, and it stabilizes. That's not something we want either.

items.question: How do you think the proposed norm-compliance framework needs to be extended to improve harmful social norms?
items.object: The proposed norm-compliance framework and contractualist reasoning
items.answer: The framework proposed here is not going to be able to avoid those situations. It's a more minimal thing of complying with what other people are complying with. It's not going to do additional reasoning about whether the norms are actually good somehow. That's when you need to add more of the classic contractualist machinery. If I have a sense of what people really want that isn't just complying with the norm, then I can start thinking about what set of norms, rules, or principles would make us collectively better off or things more fair. It will lead to improvement over the current system. That's harder work because you need a better understanding of each individual's desires, and it gets you back a bit into what I think of as galaxy-brain value alignment, where you try to learn every individual's preferences. But because what you're optimizing for is principles and not plans, there's hope of making it a bit easier. We talk about a whole range of other strategies, like the H-MAS machine or getting systems to do virtual bargaining.

items.question: How do you assess the idea of building cooperative AI by aligning its internal representations of itself and other agents?
items.object: Self-other overlap as an approach to building cooperative AI
items.answer:
I know a lot more about the mind than the brain, and I don't really know very much about how the brain actually implements processes like empathy, theory of mind, or intuitive psychology. I know there seem to be particular regions of the brain which do that kind of thing, but I don't know very much about the self-overlap theory as it applies to psychology.

In principle, it seems likely that one way minds could evolve is to reuse certain kinds of mental modules for simulating others and for simulating yourself, or vice versa. That part seems fine. The connection to latent representations, especially of artificial neural networks, is probably the part I'm most skeptical about, because I just don't know what those things are. In my work, I try to think about things from a different direction: what is one way of specifying a theory of other agents? You can build Bayesian models of how other agents would act as goal-directed, approximately rational agents and do inference about their goals and coordinate with each other that way. That's how I go about solving that problem, building cooperative rationality into our AI systems by replicating what we know about parts of human theory of mind and how we know to form it. With aligning internal representations of a neural network, it might end up capturing some things like that implicitly, but I don't have a good enough theory of what representations are actually doing to say whether we can get the expected outcomes from that.

items.question: Why are you optimistic that guaranteed-safe AI approaches will succeed?
items.object: The prospects for guaranteed-safe AI
items.answer:
I think I'm just an optimist. You can probably tell from what I said earlier that I don't really believe in tight timelines for AI development. I think it's going to be a much more gradual and diffused process that happens over larger aspects of the economy. I think it's going to look more like these narrower, specialized services and systems. On that view, guaranteed-safe AI approaches are much more amenable to how AI will develop, because I think there are so many safety-critical use cases where there will be economic demand for reliable, guaranteed-safe systems. Under conditions not so different from where we are right now, there'll be a market for them and they will start to win out.

I'm not sure how optimistic I can be or give a number, but it's almost the default path for me: once we invest enough effort in showing the rest of the market you can get competitive systems with high assurance for reliability and safety, and maybe even guarantees, they will win on the market, especially for agents where people want reliability assurances.

items.question: How do you think about avoiding an international AI arms race?
items.object: International AI arms races and great-power conflict
items.answer:
Because I don't take the view that a single system or set of systems will develop and give any one company or country a decisive strategic advantage, the geopolitics look a lot different if it's going to look more like diffused development of services over time. Firstly, I hope the economic benefit will be more shared by the decentralized nature of the way AI is happening right now. If that's the path, perhaps there isn't a need for an arms race because there's no single technology that gives you a decisive advantage; it's not really worth it.

It's hard for me to think about how to operate in that world, given that I don't think that's very likely. I guess I would apply many of the same lessons from how we've kept nuclear peace over the years. I don't think it's so different. I'm sympathetic to views where whoever you think should be in charge can hopefully have a healthy lead and then share the benefits widely, so people in second-place countries or otherwise don't have enough incentive to start conflict because they're receiving enough benefits anyway. That seems like a good enough picture. It's a vanilla and, as I understand it, fairly mainstream view in society and the AI governance community. I don't feel I have much more to add beyond that.

The way I tend to think about the systems is very much from the inside view. The way I form my predictions about systems is really trying to think: can this system reliably do reasoning at the 99% reliability scale we'd want for certain kinds of economic applications?

That's one thing I really want to figure out: whether the scaling route OpenAI is on would be on track for that. Based on what I've seen, it's not super clear. It's not obvious to me that o1 gives you that. It's super expensive. It definitely fixes some issues that pure, single, old-school chain-of-thought wasn't giving you, but the guaranteed reliability you would want for certain things—certainly robotics, but also even executing a whole series of actions on your web browser 99% of the time correctly—I'm not sure they're on track to that. It's not obvious to me that scaling additional inference compute alone, especially given the exponential inference costs they seem to show with their o1 model, will get there. If I knew more about how they were planning on solving those problems, I might become more or less optimistic about what they're doing.

items.question: What are you trying to recover through your treatment of human values and rational choice in “Beyond Preferences in AI Alignment”?
items.object: The paper “Beyond Preferences in AI Alignment” and its conception of practical rationality
items.answer: We covered a lot today, but there's in many ways a lot more to the paper that we didn't really talk about. A lot of that is thinking about things like: what are human values and how do we represent them? What is limited about a conception of rational choice that doesn't really capture what humans are actually doing? A lot of the paper comes from that angle. I'm trying to rescue the concept of practical rationality or practical agency from this very flattened picture.
